items.name: Penicillin
clues: Often called the luckiest accident in the history of medicine. Before it, an infected cut could kill you.
A laboratory at St Mary’s Hospital in London, in 1928.
A scientist from a farm in Ayrshire, in Scotland, who was famously not the tidiest person in the lab.
He came back from a summer holiday and found mould growing on one of his dishes of bacteria. Around the mould, the bacteria had died.
It was mass-produced during the Second World War, and its discoverer shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.
The first antibiotic, named after the Penicillium mould.

items.name: Aspirin
clues: One of the most used medicines in history: for headaches, for fevers and, in small daily doses, for some people’s hearts.
A chemical company in Elberfeld, now part of Wuppertal, in 1897.
A young chemist called Felix Hoffmann. The story goes that he wanted something gentler for his father’s rheumatism.
People had used willow bark and meadowsweet against pain for thousands of years. The chemist made a stable form of their active ingredient.
Its maker registered the name as a trademark in March 1899. The company is now based in Leverkusen.
A for acetyl, spir for the meadowsweet plant, and -in because drug names ending in -in were fashionable.

items.name: X-rays
clues: For the first time, doctors could see inside a living body without cutting it open.
Würzburg, November 1895.
A physics professor who went on to win the very first Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1901.
He was experimenting with a glass tube in a darkened room when a screen nearby began to glow.
One of the first pictures showed his wife’s hand, bones and wedding ring. When she saw it, she said: “I have seen my death.”
He named them after the letter mathematicians use for an unknown. In German they are named after him.

items.name: Smallpox vaccine
clues: The reason one of humanity’s deadliest diseases no longer exists anywhere except in a couple of laboratories.
A village in Gloucestershire, in England, in 1796.
A country doctor who had heard that milkmaids hardly ever caught a terrible disease.
He took material from a sore on a milkmaid’s hand and put it into a small cut on the arm of his gardener’s eight-year-old son.
In 1980 the World Health Organization declared the disease it prevents completely gone: the first human disease ever eradicated.
The word comes from vacca, Latin for cow, because it all started with cowpox.

items.name: Insulin
clues: It turned an illness that killed children within months or a few years into one that people live with for decades.
The University of Toronto, 1921 to 1922.
A young surgeon and a medical student, working through one hot summer, mostly on experiments with dogs.
In January 1922 a 14-year-old boy who was close to death received the first injection.
Its discoverers sold the patent to their university for one dollar each. One of them said it belonged to the world.
A hormone made in the pancreas that controls blood sugar. People with type 1 diabetes inject it.

items.name: Stethoscope
clues: Probably the best-known symbol of a doctor, even though many doctors now use other machines more.
Necker Hospital, Paris, 1816.
A French doctor, René Laennec, who later died of tuberculosis, a disease his invention helped doctors to recognise.
Too embarrassed to put his ear to a young woman’s chest, he rolled a sheet of paper into a tube and listened through it.
His first versions were single wooden tubes. Today’s version has two earpieces and hangs round the doctor’s neck.
From the Greek words for ‘chest’ and ‘to look at’.
